extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (or beginning graduate) students learning real analysis / instructors using the textbook
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter covering real-number basics: suprema/infima and their algebraic behavior, maxima/minima, extended reals, absolute value and triangle inequalities, bounded functions, intervals and cardinality of R, and decimal representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suprema/infima under translation and scalar multiplication (Proposition 1.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ⊂ ℝ is nonempty and x ∈ ℝ, then sup(x + A) = x + sup A and inf(x + A) = x + inf A. If x > 0 and A bounded above, then sup(xA) = x sup A; if x > 0 and A bounded below, inf(xA) = x inf A. If x < 0 the roles of sup and inf switch: multiplying by a negative number switches supremum for an infimum and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via translating upper bounds; watch sign of scalar: multiply-by-negative flips order. Examples: adding 5 to set adds 5 to its sup/inf; 3A example given. Exercise: remaining parts left to reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone relation of sup A and inf B when elements compare (Proposition 1.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A, B ⊂ ℝ are nonempty such that x ≤ y whenever x ∈ A and y ∈ B, then A is bounded above, B bounded below, and sup A ≤ inf B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that any element of B is a lower bound for B etc.; warns that x < y for all elements does not force sup A < inf B necessarily (strictness subtle). Example given with A = {−1/n} and B = {1/n} showing sup A = inf B = 0 despite x < y always.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation of supremum by elements (Proposition 1.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S ⊂ ℝ is nonempty and bounded above, then for every ε > 0 there exists x ∈ S such that sup S − ε < x ≤ sup S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard characterization of least upper bound: elements of S can be found arbitrarily close below the sup. (A similar statement holds for infima.) Exercise: prove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions for sup/inf on empty or unbounded sets (Definition 1.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend sup/inf so they are defined without worrying about emptiness/unboundedness: sup ∅ = −∞; if A not bounded above then sup A = ∞; inf ∅ = ∞; if A not bounded below then inf A = −∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce extended real line ℝ* = ℝ ∪ {−∞, ∞} with the obvious order −∞ < x < ∞ for all x ∈ ℝ. Warning: do not perform arbitrary arithmetic with ±∞ (e.g., ∞ − ∞ undefined). ℝ* is not a field; used sparingly in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxima and minima (1.2.4 discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: When A is bounded above and sup A ∈ A, then sup A is the maximum of A (max A). Similarly, when A is bounded below and inf A ∈ A, use min A notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite sets supremum and infimum coincide with max/min and are elements of the set; use max/min to emphasize the extremum lies in the set. Example: max{1,2.4,π,100}=100, min=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute value definition (start of §1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute value |x| defined by |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and |x| = −x if x < 0. Think of |x| as the 'size' of a real number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout as measure of magnitude; motivates later inequalities and boundedness concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of absolute value (Proposition 1.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Main properties: (i) |x| = 0 iff x = 0. (ii) |−x| = |x|. (iii) |xy| = |x| |y|. (iv) |x| ≥ 0. (v) If |x| ≤ y ??? (text lists standard inequalities). (vi) x^2 = |x|^2 etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition lists standard algebraic consequences (negation, product, square). Many small inequalities follow and are used to prove the triangle inequality; proofs by case analysis on sign of operands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality (Proposition 1.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For all x,y ∈ ℝ, |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Proposition 1.3.1 and adding two inequalities after replacing variables appropriately. Fundamental tool for estimates and bounding expressions; several corollaries follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse triangle inequality and variant (Corollary 1.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) Reverse triangle inequality: ||x| − |y|| ≤ |x − y|. (ii) Other triangle variants obtained by substitutions, e.g., |x − y| + |y − z| ≥ |x − z| etc. (text shows standard derived inequalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain by plugging suitable choices into standard triangle inequality and using properties of absolute value. Useful for bounding differences and proving continuity-type estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: n-term triangle inequality (Corollary 1.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction using the two-term triangle inequality. Frequently used to bound sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded function definition and supremum/infimum of a function (Definition 1.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : D → ℝ, f is bounded if there exists M such that |f(x)| ≤ M for all x ∈ D. Define sup_D f = sup{f(x): x ∈ D} and inf_D f = inf{f(x): x ∈ D}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: polynomial restricted to closed bounded interval is bounded; same polynomial on ℝ need not be. Figure illustrates function, bound M, and sup/inf. Use extended reals to drop boundedness requirement if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of suprema/infima for pointwise inequalities (Proposition 1.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g : D → ℝ and f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ∈ D, then sup_D f ≤ sup_D g and inf_D f ≤ inf_D g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: any upper bound for g is an upper bound for f, so least upper bound of f ≤ least upper bound of g. Caution: the stronger inequality sup f ≤ inf g is not guaranteed unless f(x) ≤ g(y) for all x,y ∈ D (exercise/counterexample provided). Boundedness hypothesis can be dropped using extended reals (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful warning about misapplying sup/inf inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The inequality sup_D f ≤ inf_D g does not follow from pointwise f(x) ≤ g(x) unless the stronger hypothesis f(x) ≤ g(y) for all x,y ∈ D holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text provides a counterexample exercise and leaves stronger statement/proof as an exercise (Exercise 1.3.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervals: types and formal definition (start of §1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal definitions of intervals for a < b: [a,b], (a,b), [a,b), (a,b] and unbounded intervals (a,∞), [a,∞), (−∞,b), (−∞,b], and ℝ. Intervals are sets that contain all points between any two of their points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 1.4.1: I ⊂ ℝ is an interval iff I has at least two points and for all a < b in I, every c with a < c < b is in I. Note: book restricts to intervals with at least two points (excludes empty/singleton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality facts and Cantor uncountability (Theorem 1.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem (Cantor): ℝ is uncountable. Proof given by constructing a real not in any countable subset via nested intervals (contrapositive approach using sup/inf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct sequences (a_n),(b_n) narrowing down and set y = sup A; show y ∉ listed countable set. Remarks: other proofs (diagonalization) appear later; relationship of cardinalities between intervals and ℝ discussed (bijections given or sketched).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal expansions: truncations and representation (Proposition 1.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every infinite decimal digit sequence 0.d1 d2 d3 … represents a unique real x ∈ [0,1]. Conversely, for every x ∈ [0,1] there exists an infinite digit sequence representing x. Moreover, truncations D_n satisfy D_n ≤ x ≤ D_n + 10^{−n} for all n, and there is a unique representation satisfying D_n < x for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction of digits uses Archimedean property; uniqueness holds if we require truncations strictly less than x (prevents trailing 9 ambiguity). The only nonunique cases are numbers with a terminating decimal (infinite trailing 0s) vs the alternate representation ending with infinite 9s (e.g., 0.5000… = 0.49999…).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonalization proof of uncountability of [0,1] (Theorem 1.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any countable list x_n = 0.d_{n1} d_{n2} d_{n3} … construct y = 0.e1 e2 e3 … where e_n ≠ d_{nn} (choose e_n ∈ {1,2} depending on d_{nn}). Then y differs from x_n in the nth digit, so y is not in the list; hence [0,1] is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard diagonalization trick. Ensure using unique representations (avoid using terminating representations on diagonal to prevent collisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational numbers have eventually repeating decimal expansions (Proposition 1.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x = p/q is rational with integers p,q > 0 then the decimal digits of x eventually repeat: there exist N and period P such that for all n ≥ N, d_{n+P} = d_n. The period P is at most q (bounded by number of possible remainders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by long division: remainders take only finitely many values 0..q−1 so remainders must repeat, yielding periodic digits. Converse (periodic decimal ⇒ rational) left as exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of nonunique decimal representations
rubrics_metrics.description: A real x ∈ [0,1] has two decimal representations iff x can be written as m / 10^n for integers m,n (i.e., has a terminating expansion). In that case exactly two representations exist: one ending with infinite zeros and one ending with infinite nines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained in Proposition 1.5.1 proof and remarks; example 1/2 = 0.5000… = 0.49999…. Exercises ask to classify and prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example of an explicitly constructed irrational via digits (Example 1.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number x = 0.101001000100001000001… with n zeros then a 1 then n+1 zeros etc. is irrational because its decimal digits never become eventually periodic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Proposition 1.5.3 contrapositive: digits not eventually repeating implies irrational; the example illustrates constructing explicit nonrepeating decimal.
